videos.description:
We've all seen the movies and heard the hype: But is it really possible to bring back animals that have gone extinct? If so, how? And how soon? And can I have a mammoth to ride around in my backyard? RESOURCES:

- McClain et al. 2019, the original alligator fall experiment at ~2,000 m: isopods on the first carcass within 43 hours, the second stripped to bone by day 51, and the third gone after 8 days with the 45 lb harness and weight dragged 8 m (the large elasmobranch suggestion). Also the source for the deep-sea carbon-deficit motivation: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0225345 and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6924670
- Bryant, Nunnally, Hanks & McClain 2022, the sediment study around the 19.5 kg alligator. It found up to three times more carbon than background sediment and argues that the size threshold for enriching sediments is lower than assumed: https://doi.org/10.1111/maec.12707
- Berman, Hiley, Read & Rouse 2024, the formal description of Osedax craigmcclaini from the alligator bones, and Osedax bozoi from cow bones at the same Gulf depth (Zootaxa 5443(3): 337–352): https://doi.org/10.11646/zootaxa.5443.3.2 and https://zenodo.org/record/11045291
- Danise & Higgs 2015, Osedax borings in ~100-million-year-old plesiosaur and sea turtle bones, showing the worms fed on marine reptile falls before whales existed: https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2015.0072 and https://pearl.plymouth.ac.uk/handle/10026.1/3329
- Smith, Glover, Treude, Higgs & Amon 2015, the whale-fall review covering successional stages, bone lipids and whale falls as evolutionary stepping stones: https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-marine-010213-135144 and https://core.ac.uk/works/100908260
- McClain, Nunnally, Chapman & Barry 2018, the 5-year wood fall experiment at 3,203 m, where more wood meant more species: https://par.nsf.gov/servlets/purl/10166878
- McClain & Barry 2014, wood fall community composition tracking energy availability: https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2014.0129
- Bienhold et al. 2013, how deep-sea wood falls sustain chemosynthetic life: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0053590
- Smith et al. 2016, the 27-year abyssal Pacific time series where sinking carbon met only about 63% of seafloor demand, for the carbon-deficit point: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7175715

videos.title: Every Known Megatheropod | Evolution’s Answer to Dragons
videos.description:
Megatheropods were the biggest predators to ever walk on land in Earth’s history. From their humble origins as medium-sized hunters in the Triassic, theropods developed into many different types of hunters and even herbivores, filling niches from bone-crushing giants to plant-and-fish-eating lake-lovers. A megatheropod is defined here as an animal descended from the most recent common ancestor of Coelophysis and birds whose adult body mass meets or exceeds five thousand kilograms, or five metric tonnes. That’s eleven thousand pounds, for my fellow Americans who don’t know what the flip a kilometer is. And today, we’re going to discuss the ecology, biology, and evolution of the megatheropod kingdom, with each animal sorted into mass-based tiers, because dinosaur nerds like me are suckers for that kind of thing. Whether you want fun facts to tell your friends or obsessively calculated mass estimates to repost on Discord, I’ve got you covered.

videos.title: When Whales Could Walk | Full Documentary | NOVA | PBS
videos.description:
Giant fossils uncovered in the Sahara Desert reveal new secrets of how whales evolved.

Official Website: https://to.pbs.org/3S9epv9 | #novapbs 

In Egypt’s Sahara Desert, massive skeletons with strange skulls and gigantic teeth jut out from the sandy ground. This fossil graveyard, millions of years old, is known as the “Valley of the Whales.” Now, paleontologists have unearthed a whole new species of ancient whale dating to 43 million years ago, and this predator wasn’t just able to swim – it also had four legs and could walk. Follow scientists as they search for new clues to the winding evolutionary path of mammals that moved from the land into the sea to become the largest animals on Earth.

Spanish subtitles and dubbing now available! To access these, click the gear icon at the bottom right of the video and change the audio track and subtitles to Spanish.

videos.title: How Ancient Whales May Have Changed the Deep Ocean
videos.description:
Check out American Veteran: Keep It Close on @PBSDocumentaries: https://youtu.be/9lc1sMaQOQQ
